meta.title: Who really said "A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back when it begins to rain"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Robert Frost. Quote Investigator traces this banking proverb to 1905 and anonymous print by 1930; a 1949 quotation dictionary first put Frost's name on it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back when it begins to rain'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Robert Frost. The joke was anonymous in print by 1930 and unattributed in 1934; Evan Esar's 1949 quotation dictionary invented the Frost credit.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — an anonymous banking proverb
answer.authorDates: Kernel in print by 1905 · full saying circulating anonymously by 1930
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the idea to an unnamed bank customer quoted in The Accountant (London) on 15 April 1905, and the full saying to anonymous print in 1930; Barry Popik records this near-exact wording running unattributed in the Ottawa Citizen on 24 October 1934. Robert Frost’s name was first attached in 1949, when the quotation compiler Evan Esar credited him in The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations — a reference-book ascription with no source behind it, and none has ever been found in Frost’s poems, prose, letters or recorded talks.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Accountant, London, 15 April 1905 — the idea, credited to an unnamed bank customer
The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago, January 1930 — introduced as the work of “some person of shrewd wit”
Ottawa Citizen, 24 October 1934, page 19 (recorded by Barry Popik)
The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations, Evan Esar, 1949

source.excerpt: Some person of shrewd wit has given a definition of a banker which, though a bit severe, nevertheless strikes a responsive chord. A banker, according to this definition, is a fellow who lends you his umbrella when the sun is shining and insists upon its return as soon as it starts to rain.
trail: 1905 — the earliest instance Quote Investigator found is not a quip by anyone famous but a complaint: a chartered accountant’s paper in The Accountant (London) reports a customer telling him, “You bankers only lend a man an umbrella when it is a fine day” — see the citation ↗.

1930 — the saying reaches its modern shape in two independent printings that year, in The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago and The International Digest, both presenting it as an anonymous jest rather than anyone’s line — both reproduced by QI ↗.
1934 — the wording asked about here appears almost verbatim in the Ottawa Citizen of 24 October, with no author named at all, in Barry Popik’s citation file ↗.

1944, then 1949 — Bennett Cerf hands the joke to Mark Twain in Try and Stop Me; five years later Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations splits the honours, giving one version to Twain and this one to Robert Frost. That entry is the origin of the Frost credit, and it cites nothing — QI reproduces both entries ↗.
source.excerptNote: From Lionel D. Edie’s article on the 1929 crash in The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago, as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗. Note what the writer does not do: an economist introducing the saying in 1930 credits it to “some person of shrewd wit” rather than to a famous name — because in 1930 there was no famous name to credit.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording. The saying is anonymous: the versions that are safely out of copyright — the 1905 remark in The Accountant and the 1930 printings — are worded differently from the line asked about here, while this phrasing is first documented in an unattributed 1934 newspaper item and, in its Frost-credited form, in Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations of 1949, a compilation published in copyright. With no identifiable author and no single work that can be called its first publication, quotle.info makes no public-domain claim.

author.name: Robert Frost
author.kicker: Popularly credited — but not the source
author.heading: About the poet whose name got attached
author.metaLine: 1874–1963 · American poet · four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry
author.bio: Robert Frost was born in San Francisco on 26 March 1874 and died in Boston on 29 January 1963. He remains the only poet to win four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry — for New Hampshire (1924), Collected Poems (1931), A Further Range (1937) and A Witness Tree (1943) — and wrote “The Road Not Taken,” “Mending Wall” and “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening.” At 86 he appeared at John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inauguration, where sunlight on the page defeated him and he recited “The Gift Outright” from memory instead. None of that includes the banker joke. Frost wrote about walls, woods and work, not about credit markets, and the saying was already old and unsigned before any compiler thought to put his name on it.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest instance of the underlying saying, per Quote Investigator: John Moodie, “Notes on a Banker’s Accounts,” The Accountant (London), 15 April 1905, 464 — “You bankers only lend a man an umbrella when it is a fine day,” there credited to an unnamed customer. The Robert Frost ascription first appears in Evan Esar, The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1949). Chronology: Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: A Banker Lends You His Umbrella When It’s Sunny and Wants It Back When It Rains,” 7 April 2011, quoteinvestigator.com ↗.

copyAttribution: "A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back when it begins to rain." — not Robert Frost. It is an anonymous banking proverb. Quote Investigator traces the idea to a bank customer quoted in The Accountant (London), 15 April 1905, and the full saying to anonymous print by 1930; Barry Popik records this wording unattributed in the Ottawa Citizen, 24 October 1934. Frost's name first appears on it in Evan Esar's Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949). Mark Twain, Ambrose Bierce, Ralph Waldo Emerson and Philip La Follette have all been credited too. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Four famous names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb that collects celebrities. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the saying in circulation for decades before any famous person was named, after which compilers and columnists attached whichever wit came to mind.

items.why: The credit begins with Evan Esar’s The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949), which gave Twain one version and Frost another — “A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back again when it begins to rain” — with no source attached, as Quote Investigator documents ↗. Barry Popik’s file shows the same wording running in the Ottawa Citizen in 1934 with nobody’s name on it, and a 1950 banking handbook repeating the Frost credit only as what the poet “is quoted as having described” — second-hand from the start.

Bennett Cerf put it in Twain’s mouth in Try and Stop Me (1944), five years before Esar reached Frost. Twain’s own custodians reject it: TwainQuotes ↗ files the line with the note that until the attribution can be verified, “the quote should not be regarded as authentic.”
Ben Bernanke and Mark Gertler credited Bierce in a 1999 Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City paper — the saying’s highest-status outing, and still an attribution QI finds no basis for ↗.

items.who: Ralph Waldo Emerson and Philip La Follette
items.why: Barry Popik’s chronology records the line credited to Emerson in a 1984 American Bar Association Journal piece and to the former Wisconsin governor Philip La Follette in a 1987 history of the Cleveland City Club — four claimants for one anonymous joke ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion is blunt: “the first instances of this maxim are anonymous. Years later, famous people such as Mark Twain, Robert Frost, and Ambrose Bierce were implausibly attached to the quotation” — read the full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why this joke keeps coming back
lead: The saying survives because it is the shortest true thing anyone has said about secured lending: credit is easiest to get when you least need it. That is why it has been redeployed in every downturn since the 1930s — and why it keeps acquiring a famous signature, because a line that good feels like it must belong to someone.

It has been laundered through serious writing too. In a 1999 Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City paper on monetary policy and asset prices, Ben Bernanke and Mark Gertler used the adage to illustrate credit-market frictions — and credited it to the satirist Ambrose Bierce, a fourth name with no better claim than Frost’s.
context.detailsSummary: The wording you have is itself a trimmed variant
detailsBody: Evan Esar’s 1949 entry, as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗, reads “ask for it back again when it begins to rain.” The version that circulates today has quietly dropped the “again.” So the string most often presented as a Robert Frost quotation is not even identical to the only Frost-credited wording anyone has ever documented.

The 1934 Ottawa Citizen printing recorded by Barry Popik ↗ ends “ask for it back the moment it begins to rain,” with no author’s name at all — the ordinary behaviour of a proverb, which drifts in wording precisely because nobody owns it.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's earliest citation is 1905-04-15, The Accountant (London): "You bankers only lend a man an umbrella when it is a fine day", said by a customer; the January 1930 Journal of Business of the University of Chicago prints the full saying credited to "some person of shrewd wit"; Bennett Cerf credited Mark Twain in 1944 (Try and Stop Me); Evan Esar's 1949 Dictionary of Humorous Quotations gave one version to Twain and "A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back again when it begins to rain" to Robert Frost; Bernanke and Gertler credited Ambrose Bierce in a 1999 FRB Kansas City paper; QI concludes the first instances are anonymous and that Twain, Frost and Bierce were "implausibly attached".

Popik calls the saying "of unknown authorship", lists Ralph Waldo Emerson, Mark Twain, Robert Frost and Philip La Follette as claimants, and records: 24 October 1934, Ottawa Citizen p.19 — "A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back the moment it begins to rain" (unattributed); 1950, C. G. McDavitt, If you're a bank director, p.37 — "Robert Frost, New England's poet laureat, is quoted as having described a bank as…"; July 1984 American Bar Association Journal — credited to Emerson; 1987 America's Soapbox — credited to Philip La Follette.

TwainQuotes.com's Banker page carries "A banker is a fellow who lends you his umbrella when the sun is shining and wants it back the minute it begins to rain" with the note: "This quote has been attributed to Mark Twain, but until the attribution can be verified, the quote should not be regarded as authentic."

Goodreads carries "A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back when it begins to rain" credited to Robert Frost with no source citation, alongside its notice that quotes are added by the community and are not verified by Goodreads.

Robert Frost was born 26 March 1874 in San Francisco and died 29 January 1963 in Boston; he was the only poet to receive four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry (New Hampshire 1924, Collected Poems 1931, A Further Range 1937, A Witness Tree 1943); he wrote "The Road Not Taken", "Mending Wall" and "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening"; at 86 he recited "The Gift Outright" from memory at Kennedy's 1961 inauguration after sunlight prevented him reading "Dedication".
Wikiquote's Robert Frost page does not contain the banker/umbrella saying in any section (checked 9 September 2026).
